I don't really count how often it happens because it feels like it's always there, making it impossible to focus on job applications.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that these worries and feelings of being overwhelmed are interfering with your daily activities and relationships, such as your work on music or interactions with your wife?\n\nPatient: Yes, they're completely disrupting everything. I've missed important job application deadlines, lost track of bills, and pulled back from my friends and the community center. My wife is really worried, and our relationship and finances are suffering because I just feel totally stuck in place.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there was a specific stressful event or change in your life that triggered these feelings of worry and being overwhelmed, or did they seem to develop more gradually over time?\n\nPatient: I've actually cycled through these kinds of ups and downs for years, but this current bad stretch was triggered about three months ago when a long-term freelance contract fell through. Losing that income caused our bills to pile up, and the sudden financial stress just completely shut me down.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that your current struggles began about three months ago after losing a freelance contract, but you've had similar ups and downs for years. Can you describe how your response to this recent stressor differs from your past experiences with stress and anxiety?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure how it differs, other than the fact that this time the financial pressure feels much heavier and more urgent. The consequences have become so much more severe and disruptive, like falling behind on our rent and missing deadlines for jobs I really need. In the past, I guess I always managed to scrape by, but now it feels like I'm completely stuck.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any periods of persistent elevated mood, increased energy, or decreased need for sleep, where you felt extremely productive or creative, especially when working on your music?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely get into these \"up phases\" or \"high gears\" where I only sleep three or four hours a night but wake up buzzing and feeling totally fine. During those times, I'm incredibly amped up and restless, staying up late tweaking music, sketching business plans, and feeling like I have this special grind mode that can solve our money problems overnight. My wife says I start talking a mile a minute and jumping from one idea to the next without even taking a breath.\n\nDoctor: During these 'up phases,' do you ever find yourself engaging in impulsive or risky behaviors, such as excessive spending or reckless decisions, that might be problematic when you're back to your normal self?\n\nPatient: I don't really engage in reckless or dangerous things like wild spending sprees or physical risks during those times. Instead, my impulsivity is mostly limited to overcommitting to too many projects, signing up for online courses, or staying up all night planning businesses.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often these 'up phases' occur and how long they typically last, as this might help us understand the pattern of your mood swings?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure about the exact duration or how often they happen, since I've never really tracked the number of days. They just seem to come and go on and off, and I usually only realize it's happening when I'm already in the middle of it.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience significant depressive episodes that last for at least two weeks, where you feel persistently down, hopeless, or lose interest in activities you once enjoyed, separate from your worries about finances and daily life?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely get those heavy, shutdown lows, and they last much longer than two weeks—this current stretch has been dragging on for about three months, and I've been cycling through them since my early twenties. During these times, I wake up with a sinking feeling in my chest, feel like my wife would be better off without me, and completely lose interest in my music or coding.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your 'up phases' and low periods are related, if at all, and whether you've noticed any pattern or trigger that switches you from one state to the other?\n\nPatient: I've been cycling between those high-energy bursts and heavy lows since my early twenties, but they've become much more severe and disruptive lately. Stress is definitely a major trigger for me, and losing that long-term contract three months ago created a ton of financial pressure that pushed me right into this current, long low phase.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your 'up phases' and low periods occur in a distinct, episodic pattern, with clear periods of normal mood in between, or if they tend to blend together or occur simultaneously?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure about the exact pattern. Historically, they felt like distinct phases with some normal periods in between, but lately, under all this financial stress, the transitions have felt much faster or more blurred. It's made it really hard to find any kind of stable middle ground.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the number of distinct episodes of both your 'up phases' and low periods over the past year, to help clarify the pattern and frequency of these mood swings?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure of the exact number of episodes over the past year, as they tend to blur together quite a bit. But I definitely know I've been cycling back and forth between those highs and lows pretty frequently.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to approximate how many times you've switched between these 'up phases' and low periods in the past year, even if it's just a rough estimate?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure of the exact number of times I've switched because it's just too hard to keep track of. It has been happening on and off, and it definitely feels like it has become more frequent lately.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to recall if there have been any periods, even brief, where you felt completely normal, without either the high-energy 'up phases' or the low periods, over the past year?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest. It feels like I've just been constantly bouncing between the highs and the lows lately, without much of a normal middle ground in between.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any specific factors or events that might have contributed to the increased frequency or severity of your mood swings over the past year, such as significant life changes, medical conditions, or substance use?\n\nPatient: The major trigger has definitely been the severe financial pressure, especially after a long-term freelance contract was canceled a few months ago, which caused us to fall behind on rent and pushed me into this current low. On top of that, the ongoing stress of trying to secure a stable job over the last couple of years has made these cycles much more noticeable and disruptive.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a period where your 'up phase' and low period occurred simultaneously or very closely together, rather than distinctly separate episodes?\n\nPatient: I don't think I've ever experienced the high and low phases at the exact same time, as they usually feel like separate periods that I cycle back and forth between. Although, I do sometimes feel both amped up and highly irritable or on edge at the same time.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you have experienced any episodes of abnormally elevated or expansive mood that lasted for at least four consecutive days, as opposed to the longer periods of low mood you've described?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely experience those high-energy, amped-up phases, and they typically last for several days at a time, usually around a week or at least four consecutive days. During those shorter \"up\" times, I get a massive surge of restless energy, stay up late working on projects, and barely need sleep, which is a sharp contrast to my heavy low periods that drag on for months before I crash.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your 'up phases' typically last for less than four days or if they often meet or exceed the four-day mark, and how this duration might compare to your low periods?\n\nPatient: I'm not completely sure of the exact number of days my up phases typically last, but they are definitely much shorter than my low periods. My current low stretch has been dragging on for about three months now, whereas those high-energy bursts seem to come and go much more quickly, though I haven't tracked the exact day count.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your 'up phases' usually last for at least four consecutive days, and how the duration of these episodes compares to the length of your low periods?\n\nPatient: I'm really not quite sure about the exact number of days those up phases last or how they compare in length to the low periods. I haven't tracked the specific duration of those high periods closely, so it's hard to say for sure.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to estimate or recall if most of your 'up phases' last at least four consecutive days, or are they usually shorter than that?"
  }

I don't really count how often it happens because it feels like it's always there, making it impossible to focus on job applications.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that these worries and feelings of being overwhelmed are interfering with your daily activities and relationships, such as your work on music or interactions with your wife?\n\nPatient: Yes, they're completely disrupting everything. I've missed important job application deadlines, lost track of bills, and pulled back from my friends and the community center. My wife is really worried, and our relationship and finances are suffering because I just feel totally stuck in place.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there was a specific stressful event or change in your life that triggered these feelings of worry and being overwhelmed, or did they seem to develop more gradually over time?\n\nPatient: I've actually cycled through these kinds of ups and downs for years, but this current bad stretch was triggered about three months ago when a long-term freelance contract fell through. Losing that income caused our bills to pile up, and the sudden financial stress just completely shut me down.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that your current struggles began about three months ago after losing a freelance contract, but you've had similar ups and downs for years. Can you describe how your response to this recent stressor differs from your past experiences with stress and anxiety?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure how it differs, other than the fact that this time the financial pressure feels much heavier and more urgent. The consequences have become so much more severe and disruptive, like falling behind on our rent and missing deadlines for jobs I really need. In the past, I guess I always managed to scrape by, but now it feels like I'm completely stuck.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any periods of persistent elevated mood, increased energy, or decreased need for sleep, where you felt extremely productive or creative, especially when working on your music?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely get into these \"up phases\" or \"high gears\" where I only sleep three or four hours a night but wake up buzzing and feeling totally fine. During those times, I'm incredibly amped up and restless, staying up late tweaking music, sketching business plans, and feeling like I have this special grind mode that can solve our money problems overnight. My wife says I start talking a mile a minute and jumping from one idea to the next without even taking a breath.\n\nDoctor: During these 'up phases,' do you ever find yourself engaging in impulsive or risky behaviors, such as excessive spending or reckless decisions, that might be problematic when you're back to your normal self?\n\nPatient: I don't really engage in reckless or dangerous things like wild spending sprees or physical risks during those times. Instead, my impulsivity is mostly limited to overcommitting to too many projects, signing up for online courses, or staying up all night planning businesses.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how often these 'up phases' occur and how long they typically last, as this might help us understand the pattern of your mood swings?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure about the exact duration or how often they happen, since I've never really tracked the number of days. They just seem to come and go on and off, and I usually only realize it's happening when I'm already in the middle of it.\n\nDoctor: Do you experience significant depressive episodes that last for at least two weeks, where you feel persistently down, hopeless, or lose interest in activities you once enjoyed, separate from your worries about finances and daily life?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely get those heavy, shutdown lows, and they last much longer than two weeks—this current stretch has been dragging on for about three months, and I've been cycling through them since my early twenties. During these times, I wake up with a sinking feeling in my chest, feel like my wife would be better off without me, and completely lose interest in my music or coding.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your 'up phases' and low periods are related, if at all, and whether you've noticed any pattern or trigger that switches you from one state to the other?\n\nPatient: I've been cycling between those high-energy bursts and heavy lows since my early twenties, but they've become much more severe and disruptive lately. Stress is definitely a major trigger for me, and losing that long-term contract three months ago created a ton of financial pressure that pushed me right into this current, long low phase.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your 'up phases' and low periods occur in a distinct, episodic pattern, with clear periods of normal mood in between, or if they tend to blend together or occur simultaneously?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure about the exact pattern. Historically, they felt like distinct phases with some normal periods in between, but lately, under all this financial stress, the transitions have felt much faster or more blurred. It's made it really hard to find any kind of stable middle ground.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the number of distinct episodes of both your 'up phases' and low periods over the past year, to help clarify the pattern and frequency of these mood swings?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure of the exact number of episodes over the past year, as they tend to blur together quite a bit. But I definitely know I've been cycling back and forth between those highs and lows pretty frequently.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to approximate how many times you've switched between these 'up phases' and low periods in the past year, even if it's just a rough estimate?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure of the exact number of times I've switched because it's just too hard to keep track of. It has been happening on and off, and it definitely feels like it has become more frequent lately.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to recall if there have been any periods, even brief, where you felt completely normal, without either the high-energy 'up phases' or the low periods, over the past year?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, to be honest. It feels like I've just been constantly bouncing between the highs and the lows lately, without much of a normal middle ground in between.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any specific factors or events that might have contributed to the increased frequency or severity of your mood swings over the past year, such as significant life changes, medical conditions, or substance use?\n\nPatient: The major trigger has definitely been the severe financial pressure, especially after a long-term freelance contract was canceled a few months ago, which caused us to fall behind on rent and pushed me into this current low. On top of that, the ongoing stress of trying to secure a stable job over the last couple of years has made these cycles much more noticeable and disruptive.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a period where your 'up phase' and low period occurred simultaneously or very closely together, rather than distinctly separate episodes?\n\nPatient: I don't think I've ever experienced the high and low phases at the exact same time, as they usually feel like separate periods that I cycle back and forth between. Although, I do sometimes feel both amped up and highly irritable or on edge at the same time.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you have experienced any episodes of abnormally elevated or expansive mood that lasted for at least four consecutive days, as opposed to the longer periods of low mood you've described?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely experience those high-energy, amped-up phases, and they typically last for several days at a time, usually around a week or at least four consecutive days. During those shorter \"up\" times, I get a massive surge of restless energy, stay up late working on projects, and barely need sleep, which is a sharp contrast to my heavy low periods that drag on for months before I crash.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your 'up phases' typically last for less than four days or if they often meet or exceed the four-day mark, and how this duration might compare to your low periods?\n\nPatient: I'm not completely sure of the exact number of days my up phases typically last, but they are definitely much shorter than my low periods. My current low stretch has been dragging on for about three months now, whereas those high-energy bursts seem to come and go much more quickly, though I haven't tracked the exact day count.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm whether your 'up phases' usually last for at least four consecutive days, and how the duration of these episodes compares to the length of your low periods?\n\nPatient: I'm really not quite sure about the exact number of days those up phases last or how they compare in length to the low periods. I haven't tracked the specific duration of those high periods closely, so it's hard to say for sure.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to estimate or recall if most of your 'up phases' last at least four consecutive days, or are they usually shorter than that?\n\nPatient: I'm not completely sure of the exact number of days they last, since I don't really count them. But when I'm in them, they definitely feel like they go on for several days at a time.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to distinguish whether your 'up phases' are typically shorter, lasting less than four days, or if they often last four days or more, to help clarify the pattern of your mood swings?\n\nPatient: I'm not completely sure about the exact number of days my up phases last. They definitely feel like they go on for a few days at a time where I'm full of energy, but I've never tracked the precise number of days to know if it's consistently more or less than four.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to remember if there was ever a time when you had both an 'up phase' and a low period within the same month, or do they typically occur separately over longer periods of time?"
